title: "zotLook"

description: >-
  What zotLook is, what it needs, and how to install it: preview Zotero attachments with the Space key on macOS, Linux and Windows.
---

**zotLook** is a plugin for the open-source reference manager
[**Zotero**](https://www.zotero.org/). It previews the attachment of the
selected Zotero item when you press **Space**, the way a file manager does.
zotLook carries no viewer of its own; it drives the preview the system already
has:

- [**Quick Look**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quick_Look) on **macOS**,
- [**GNOME Sushi**](https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/sushi) on **Linux**,
- [**QuickLook**](https://github.com/QL-Win/QuickLook) on **Windows**.

[Whatever those can show](platforms.qmd#which-formats-appear-where), zotLook can therefore show as well. And if you [extend a preview program with plugins](platforms.qmd#extending-the-preview), you extend what zotLook can do with it.

Beyond that, **Ctrl+Shift+Space** builds a **contact sheet** of a PDF: a grid of
every page, its column count adjustable. **That helps most with long documents
such as books**, because the system's preview will show you every page but only
one or two at a time. The contact sheet zotLook builds is shown by the system
preview — and **a click on a page opens it in Zotero's reader**. Building one
can take a few seconds; a progress indicator names the page zotLook is
currently rendering.

What sets zotLook apart, besides previewing on **every platform**, is that
**Zotero's annotations become part of the preview** — in the system's preview
as well as on the contact sheet. Zotero keeps annotations in its database
rather than in the file, so a preview would normally show the document without
them. The feature can be switched off in zotLook if you would rather see the
file as it is stored.

The sheet's two menus, on macOS: the contents from the PDF's outline, the
annotations from Zotero, each entry bringing its page to the middle of the

## What you need

| | |
|---|---|
| **Zotero** | [**Zotero**](https://www.zotero.org/) **10** — the version zotLook is developed and tested against. On older ones, see below. |
| **macOS** | macOS 12 (Monterey) or later. Nothing to install, Quick Look is part of the system. |
| **Linux** | [GNOME Sushi](https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/sushi). On Debian and Ubuntu: `sudo apt install gnome-sushi`. |
| **Windows** | [QuickLook](https://github.com/QL-Win/QuickLook). The Store and website versions work alike. |

### Older versions of Zotero

zotLook still **installs** on Zotero 7 and later, and may well work there, but it
has been neither developed nor tested on 7, 8 or 9, so nothing about them is
claimed. Reading Zotero's own sources says this much:

- Everything else the plugin calls is there in **7.0.0** already —
  `zotero://open-pdf?cfi=`, `PreferencePanes.register`, `PDFWorker.export`,
  `getMainWindows`.
- `EPUB.mjs`, which the EPUB preview and the EPUB page overview are built on,
  first appears in **Zotero 8**. Below that, nothing to do with EPUB can work.
- Whether Zotero 7 keeps its bundled pdf.js where the contact sheet looks for
  it, I could not check.

If you run zotLook on an older Zotero — successfully or not — please
[say so](https://github.com/fre-ms/zotLook/issues). Reports are welcome and will
be noted here.

## Install

1. Download the latest `.xpi` from the
   [releases page](https://github.com/fre-ms/zotLook/releases).
2. In Zotero: **Tools → Add-ons**.
3. Gear icon → **Install Add-on From File…**
4. Pick the file you downloaded, then restart Zotero.

From then on Zotero checks for new versions itself and updates the plugin
without being asked.

::: {.callout-note}
zotLook installs beside Guillaume Chapron's Zotero7QuickLook rather than over
it — the two carry different plugin IDs. If you have both, disable one, or the
Space key will be claimed twice.
:::

## Getting started with zotLook

Select an item and press **Space**. If the item is a parent rather than an
attachment, zotLook picks one of its attachments — a PDF before an EPUB, and
an EPUB before anything else. You can [change that order](settings.qmd). Press
**Space** again, or **Escape**, to dismiss the preview.

**Shift+Space** previews the item's notes instead, rendered as a page.

**Ctrl+Shift+Space** builds a *contact sheet*: every page of a PDF as a
thumbnail in a scrollable grid. Clicking a page opens it in Zotero's reader at
that page. A button in each corner opens the document's contents and its
annotations, and an entry brings its page to the middle of the sheet. On a long
document the sheet takes a few seconds and says so while it works.

An EPUB gets one too, where it can. A reflowable book has no pages of its own,
but one published beside a print edition usually carries that edition's
pagination along with it — and where it does, zotLook cuts the book at those
marks and shows it a page at a time, each tile linking back into the reader. A
book carrying none says so rather than showing arbitrary slices.

If the file is stored in the cloud and not on this machine, zotLook downloads it
first rather than reporting that it is missing.

## How the annotations get into the preview

zotLook exports a copy of the PDF with your highlights, notes, areas and ink
drawn in, and previews that copy rather than the stored file. An EPUB needs no
export: zotLook reads the position Zotero stores for each annotation and marks
the passage in the page it builds from the book anyway. Highlights appear in
their colour, underlines as underlines.

Attachments that carry no annotations are recognised before any work starts,
and an export is reused until you add or change an annotation. Once made, it
costs nothing more as long as nothing changes.

If you would rather see the file as it is stored, the annotations can be kept
out of the preview under [Settings](settings.qmd).

## But Zotero already has a preview

It does, and zotLook does not replace it. The item pane shows the attachment
with its annotations on it, and needs nothing else installed at all. For *what is
this?* it is the right answer.

For looking at a document more closely it is only so much use, and was probably
never meant to be more.

- It shows **a single thumbnail**, moved through with two buttons or the arrow
  keys.
- The **thumbnail is no wider than the item pane**, its height following the
  page's proportions. There is no setting for either.
- Nothing in it can be **clicked, selected or copied** — web snapshots are the
  exception, and there selection is switched off instead.
- Zotero's own preview currently (Zotero 10) handles **four formats only: PDF,
  EPUB, web snapshot, image** — video and audio are marked in the source as
  still to come.

zotLook sets out to complement it on exactly those points: *looking at something
properly without opening it.*

- **Far larger — and as large as you like.** The preview windows of all three
  systems can be dragged to any size, and what they show scales with them.
- **Independent of the item pane**, which does not have to be open for it.
- **All of it at once.** **Ctrl+Shift+Space** builds a *contact sheet*: a
  compact overview of every page of a PDF. Where a book carries a printed
  pagination, the same holds for an EPUB.
- **To the passage you want in a couple of moves.** An EPUB preview keeps its
  contents and its annotations behind a button each, above the text; Zotero's
  preview knows only forward and back.
- **From the overview into the reader.** Opening the reader at the page you were
  looking at is a feature of Zotero's preview — there for a PDF only. zotLook
  reproduces it in its own: a click on a page opens it in the reader, **for an
  EPUB as well**.
- **A document, not a picture.** What the system's preview program allows —
  selecting text, copying it, scrolling — is thereby available for Zotero
  attachments too.
- **Broad support for file formats:** whatever the system's preview can show,
  zotLook can show. [Platforms](platforms.qmd) describes what each system
  manages on its own — and
  [that can be extended considerably](platforms.qmd#extending-the-preview).
- **One key, and gone again.** Space to look, Space or Escape to dismiss. No tab
  is opened and none has to be closed.

So zotLook and Zotero's own preview answer different questions — *what is this?*
and *let me actually look at it* — and sit well side by side.
